PREFACE


             The reprocessing of nuclear spent fuel generates highly radioactive liquid wastes (HLW)
              that must be isolated from the biosphere in very durable solid matrices. In the first part of this
          book (Chapters 1 and 2), generalities are presented on the radionuclides occurring in HLW
           and on the main characteristics and preparation methods of waste forms (glasses, ceramics,
             glass-ceramics) for the immobilization of separated or non-separated wastes. In the second
             part of this book (Chapter 3), the characteristics of two categories of long-lived radionuclides
             (135Cs and minor actinides: Np, Am, Cm) and the main matrices that have been proposed for
              their specific immobilization are reviewed. In the third part of this book (Chapter 4), to
               illustrate previous chapters, several  results are presented on ceramic and glass-ceramic
            matrices developed for the conditioning of Cs (hollandite ceramic) and minor actinides
              (zirconolite  ceramic,  zirconolite-based  glass-ceramic,  apatite-based  glass-ceramic)  and

Chapter 1


                    INTRODUCTION

              Today more than 7% of all the energy consumed in the world is produced by nuclear
          power reactors (440 reactors were in activity in 2004 around the world). Nuclear energy is
              essentially used to produce electricity and represents about 16% of the electricity produced in
             the world. For this application, about 50 000 tons of natural uranium are consumed every year
            producing 11 000 tons of nuclear spent fuel [1]. For several countries (France, Belgium,
             Lithuania), the contribution of nuclear energy to electricity production is higher than 50%
                (e.g., nearly 80% for France) [2]. Even if a small number of countries in Western Europe have
          made the choice not to develop nuclear energy (Italy, Austria) or to give up progressively
              their nuclear power  activity (Germany, Sweden, Belgium)  for  political  reasons,  other
             countries have  decided  either  to  continue  to  use  nuclear  reactors  (France,  Finland,
            Switzerland) or to significantly increase the part of nuclear energy in  their  electricity
            production (China, Japan, United States, Russia, South Korea, India). The rising demand for
            energy, the risks of losing oil and gas sources of procurement and the need to reduce green-

               Today, about 30% of the nuclear spent fuel is reprocessed in the world3 [1]. The highly
             radioactive liquid wastes (HLW) arising from reprocessing are made of a complex mixture of
            both radioactive (fission products, minor actinides) and non-radioactive elements (for more
              details see Chapter 2). As they contain long-lived radionuclides (and/or long-lived daughter
            products) for which half-lives can reach thousands to millions years [7] (MA, 135Cs, 99Tc,
           93Zr…,Tables 1 and 2), HLW must be isolated from the biosphere for very long times (from
            thousands to hundreds of thousands years), at least until their radiotoxicity level drops back to
             the radiotoxicity level of the initial uranium ore (Figure 1). For instance HLW obtained after
        UOX1 (UO2 with 3.5% 235U) spent fuel reprocessing, decay to return to a level close to the
             original fuel after approximately 2 000 years (Figure 1a).
               For a very efficient immobilization, a multi-barrier concept is envisaged (waste-form <
              stainless-steel canister < engineered barrier < geological barrier) around the radioactive waste
             to  limit  the  release of  radionuclides  into  the environment through  the  action  of  the
           underground water. The increasing need for fundamental and applied studies on HLW and
            nuclear waste forms for their conditioning is thus obvious. This last point is the main topic of
              this book.
                 Currently,  after water  evaporation and  calcination  of HLW  solutions, wastes  are
            incorporated by dissolution into the structure of glasses4 (mainly calcium alkali borosilicate
             glasses but aluminophosphate glasses are also used in Russia [8,9]) melted in metallic5 or
            ceramic  melters6  at  temperature  not  exceeding  1100-1150°C  for  technical  reasons.
             Borosilicate glassy matrices are also used to immobilize the defence wastes obtained after the
            reprocessing of military spent fuel [9].
               Moreover, new glassy matrices are also envisaged to immobilize old HLW solutions
             stored in stainless steel tanks and HLW solutions that will be produced in the future in
           commercial reactors after reprocessing of new spent fuels (see §5.B and 5.C in Chapter 5).
           For instance, in France, in order to improve reactors performance, the proportion of 235U
               fissile isotope in fuel will grow in the future (high burn up UO2 fuel) [1].

             To minimize the  potential long-term impact of HLW  solutions,  investigations are
             currently in progress in several countries such as in France9 on the enhanced separation of
             several long-lived radionuclides (MA,  135Cs,  129I, 99Tc) from HLW followed by  their
            transmutation (into short-lived radionuclides or stable elements) or their immobilization in
             specific host matrices such as ceramics and glass-ceramics [20-24] more durable than current
            nuclear glasses (Figure 2).
               These long-lived radionuclides may have a major contribution to the long term potential
              radiotoxicity10  of HLW.  This  is  the  case  for MA which  are  long-lived  α-emitting
             radionuclides and that will be mainly responsible for the potential radiotoxicity of HLW after
            2-3 hundred years disposal (Figure 1).
              Even if experiments have shown the possibility to transmute MA in neutron reactors [25]
             to reduce the radiotoxic inventory, the specific immobilization of MA is considered as a
             possible alternative to transmutation. For MA immobilization, several ceramics such as
             zirconates, titanates and phosphates may incorporate higher amounts of MA in their structure
            than glasses and also exhibit better chemical resistance against water [21, 22, 26] Similarly,reserved.            highly durable matrices have also been developed for the conditioning of other highly
rights           radiotoxic actinide-rich wastes such as Pu-rich military wastes in United States and Russia
All             [9]. Other long-lived radionuclides (fission products) such as 135Cs, 129I and 99Tc have a lower
             contribution to the long-term radiotoxicity of spent fuel than MA but are more soluble in
            water and more mobile in geologic media [27-29] (Table 2). Their selective separation andIncorporated.
            immobilization in specific and highly durable matrices (hollandite, apatite…) would thus
            reduce the risks of migration towards biosphere during disposal. After enhanced separation ofPublishers,             the most problematic radionuclides occurring in HLW,  it  is planed to immobilize the
            remaining wastes (consisting of non radioactive elements, short-lived radionuclides and long-Science
             lived radionuclides with low mobility and very slightly soluble in water) in glassy matrices

             will be presented in Chapter 3. Results concerning ceramic and glass-ceramic matrices

               For an efficient immobilization,  it is expected that all the elements of the wastes are
            incorporated in the crystalline structure of the durable phases of the ceramics and not in minor
            phases segregated along grain boundaries. Consequently, all the constituent crystalline phases
           must provide sites for the variety of ion sizes and charges of all radionuclides and non
             radioactive elements of wastes. Ionic substitution may be generally possible if the ionic radii
             difference between cations does not exceed 15 % [87]. Moreover, the overall charge balance
           must be maintained in the crystals. In order to maintain local electroneutrality, multiple
              substitutional schemes can be envisaged. For instance in zirconolite (CaZrTi2O7), the partial
             substitution of Ca2+ ions by trivalent actinides or rare- earths can be achieved by substituting
              partially Ti4+ by Al3+ ions in order to compensate the positive charge excess in calcium sites
             (see Chapter  4, §4.B). Thus,  in  this example,  it appears  that  in order  to incorporate
              preferentially trivalent actinide or rare-earth ions in calcium site it is necessary to add Al2O3
             to the precursors mixture. All these  crystal chemical considerations  clearly show  that
            ceramics structure is less flexible than that of glasses to accommodate ions of various size and

              Because of both the high nucleation rate of apatite crystals in the bulk and their high
             capacity to incorporate Nd3+ cations (neodymium being a trivalent actinide surrogate), the
            glass-ceramic composition studied in this work can thus be proposed as a potential waste
           form for minor actinides and plutonium. The preference of Nd3+ cations to occupy the 6h site
             in apatite ceramics can be explained by the presence of the neighboring "free oxygen anion"
             in 2a site which does not belong to any silicate groups (Figure 14a,b)20,22. As this oxygen
            anion  is not associated with  Si4+  cations,  its doubly negative charge more  efficiently
           compensates the positive charge of trivalent lanthanide cations than that of bivalent calcium
             cations (i.e., the ionic bond is stronger between the "free oxygen anion" O2- and Nd3+ than
           between O2- and Ca2+).
             Among, the different options that were initially envisaged for immobilizing excess Pu in
            United States, it was envisaged to dissolve plutonium in a glassy matrix along with enough
              fission products (β-emitters) for non-proliferation reasons. Considering the solubility of Pu in
               silicate glasses as problematic, it was also proposed to immobilize Pu at the same time as
            neutron absorbers (for criticality control) in highly durable crystals dispersed in a glass-
            ceramic waste form. A glass-ceramic composition containing numerous crystalline phases
           and able to immobilized 17 wt% PuO2 mainly in zirconia and zirconolite phases was
           proposed [143]. It was also envisaged to incorporate simultaneously highly radioactive HLW
            wastes in this glass-ceramic to discourage recovery of the Pu.

             4.A.3.b. Structure of BaxCsy(M,Ti)8O16 Hollandite
                Natural hollandite has the formula BaMn8O16 where manganese can occur under various
             oxidation states (Mn2+, Mn3+, Mn4+). However, there are a lot of structural isotypes, including
              titanate hollandites BaxCsy(M,Ti)8O16 (x+y<2) in which Mn of natural hollandite is replaced
          by M + Ti. In our studies (§ 4.A.3.c2.), M was a trivalent cation or a mixture of different
             cations (Al3+ + Fe3+ for instance). The BaxCsy(M,Ti)8O16 type structure is shown in Figure 18.
           Approximately square tunnels running parallel to the short axis of the structure are enclosed
          by columns of two edge-sharing octahedra which then share corners. The Ti and M cations
             are located in these octahedral sites (site B). The big Ba2+ and Cs+ cations (Table 12 [182])
             are set in the tunnels in box-shaped cavities of eight oxygen ions (site A). In spite of the
              relatively open-framework-type structure of (Ba,Cs,M)-hollandite, Ba2+ and Cs+ ions have to
           overcome a large energy barrier associated with passing trough the square planar arrangement
             of oxygen ions to migrate along the axis of the tunnels and these compounds appeared as very
           bad ionic conductors4.
               Thus, the large cations are well immobilized in hollandite tunnels. Hollandite  cell
          symmetry may be tetragonal (I4/m space group) or monoclinic (I2/m space group). This
           mainly depends on the relative values of the radius of cations in sites A (rA) and B (rB) (rA and
              rB being respectively the average ionic radii of (Ba2+, Cs+) cations in site A and (M3+, Ti4+)
             cations in site B) [151, 190]. Between these two symmetries, the cross-section of the tunnels
           changes from approximately square in shape (tetragonal cell) to a rhombus shape (monoclinic
               cell). The M3+ cations in site B insured the compensation of the positive charge excess in the
             tunnels due to Cs+ and Ba2+ cations. In tetragonal hollandites, all octahedral sites B are
              identical whereas in monoclinic hollandites two different types of sites B can be distinguished
             [175]. Theoretically, a maximum of two (Ba2+ + Cs+) cations per formula unit (i.e., x+y=2)
           can be incorporated in the hollandite structure. However, it is only for small univalent cationsreserved.
            (such as K+) that the box-shaped cavities (site A) in the tunnels of hollandite can be all

            occurs as Pu4+ ions in nuclear glasses prepared under neutral or oxidizing conditions [216].
            Thus, trivalent lanthanides are not good Pu surrogates except if the Pu containing glasses are
            prepared under strongly reducing conditions (using for instance strong reducing agent such as
            Si3N4 in the melt, almost all Pu4+ ions can be reduced to Pu3+ ions [217]). The differences of
            behavior between the heaviest and the lightest actinides of HLW are due to the increase of
            nuclear charge for the heaviest actinide elements which affects the energy and the spatial
            extension of 5f orbitals. Because of the possibility to prepare materials with both Ce3+ and
           Ce4+ ions, cerium is sometimes considered as a good plutonium surrogate. Nevertheless, it
           must be underlined that cerium is easier to reduce into its trivalent state than plutonium when
             the temperature is raised during the synthesis of waste forms. Moreover, in glasses prepared
            under air, plutonium is essentially in tetravalent state whereas both Ce3+ and Ce4+ ions exist in
             these conditions [218-220]. Moreover, as neptunium exits mainly in +IV oxidation state in
             glasses melted under air [221, 222] and in zirconolite ceramics for instance [223],  it is

            considered as a good Pu4+ surrogate in spite of strong differences of solubility between Pu4+
           and Th4+ in several ceramic matrices such as ZrO2 [99].

             4.B.3.a. General Characteristics of Zirconolite
                 Zirconolite (CaZrTi2O7) is the most durable phase designed for the incorporation of
             actinides and lanthanides in Synroc phase assemblages (Table 8). For instance, zirconolite is
          more durable than perovskite (CaTiO3) [236], the other phase of Synroc able to incorporate
             actinides and lanthanides and that can form as parasitic phase during zirconolite preparation.

            (considered here as An surrogates or neutron poisons) in the Ca and Zr sites of the zirconolite
             structure will be described. In order to avoid criticality risks during disposal (particularly for
          Pu immobilization), it is interesting to note that high amounts of neutron absorbers (Gd, Hf)
           can also be introduced in zirconolite structure at the same time as actinides. Indeed, Gd and
          Hf are very good neutron absorbers with thermal neutron capture cross-sections of 49000 and
           104 barns respectively.

            (oxide route) and the wet chemistry method using alkoxide, hydroxide or nitrate precursors in
             solution (alkoxide route). The alkoxide route was largely used by the ANSTO to prepare
           Synroc [57] zirconolite-rich Synroc [273] and single phase zirconolite [274] samples. This
           wet  chemistry method was  initially developed  in  order  to  obtain a high degree  of
           homogeneity amongst the various chemical components of Synroc before heat treatments.
        CEA has  also adopted  this method  to prepare  single phase  zirconolite samples [22]
            hydrolyzing a mixture of Al, Zr and Ti alkoxides with Ca and Ln nitrates. The powder
            obtained was then dried, calcined, pressed uniaxially and sintered (1400°C 96h for instance
             for an  inactive  Ca0.8Nd0.2ZrTi1.8Al0.2O7 sample). In order  to prevent  the formation of
             perovskite as parasitic phase (that could incorporate Ln and An) a small excess of Zr and Ti
          was added in the precursors mixture but this lead to the formation of ZrTiO4 as minor phase
             in their ceramics [22]. An almost similar wet chemistry method was used by Advocat et al.

            charge  compensators  (Ca0.87Pu0.13ZrTi1.74Al0.26O7). XANES  spectroscopy  showed  that
           plutonium occurred mainly as Pu4+ in this ceramic [240].

             5.A.2.a.4. Structural Charaterization of Silicate Glasses
             As indicated above (equation (2)), by adding increasing concentrations of network-
           modifying oxides to silica glass, the average number N of NBOs per SiO4 tetrahedron
             increases. A common nomenclature is used in literature to designate the different kinds Qn of
             tetrahedra that can be present in silicate glass structure76. In this nomenclature Qn designates a
           SiO4 tetrahedron with n BOs and (4-n) NBOs. With this notation, all the tetrahedra present in
            pure  silica glass are designated as Q4 tetrahedra. A particularly powerful technique to
             characterize the structure of silicate network in simple glasses such as alkali silicate glasses is
              29Si MAS NMR spectroscopy77,78. Several characteristics of the main nuclei present in the
             structure of nuclear glasses that can be studied by MAS NMR are given in Table 33. For more
              details about MAS NMR spectroscopic studies on glasses or melts79 see for instance [341,
            385-389]. 29Si MAS NMR enables both to identify the different kinds of Qn species present in
            simple  silicate glasses by comparing their isotropic chemical  shift  δiso (in ppm)80 with
               literature data [469] (Q4(-105 < δiso < -120ppm); Q3(-91 < δiso < -102ppm); Q2(-74 < δiso < -
             94ppm))81,82 and to determine their relative concentrations by integration of the different Qn
             contributions obtained after fitting of the spectra (an example of 29Si MAS NMR curve fitting
                is shown in Figure 89).



                    76 Such a nomenclature is also used for phosphate glasses to designate the different kinds of PO4 tetrahedra.

                    spin-lattice relaxation time T1, the recording of silicon NMR spectra remains long in comparison with others
                   nuclei classically studied by NMR in simplified nuclear glasses (11B, 27Al, 23Na).

          on the cations capacity to draw off towards them the negative charge of oxygen anions): the
             polarizing effect of cations increases with their field strength making the average negative
            charge borne by the oxygen to decrease which leads to basicity decrease100. Because alkali
           and alkaline-earth cations have  relatively small polarizing  effect on oxygen anions in
           comparison with Si4+ cations, alkali and alkaline-earth oxides are strong Lewis bases whereas
           SiO2 is a Lewis acid. In silicate glasses, increasing the concentration of alkali and alkaline-
             earth oxides will thus lead to an increase of the average negative charge borne by the oxygen
            anions and of their average electron donor power (increase of glass basicity)101,102. This is
             also true for borate and phosphate glasses. When introducing high field strength (i.e., acid)
             cations such as rare-earths and actinides in silicate glasses, the glass basicity can be regarded
             as the extent to which the oxygen anions of the network can share their electron density with
             these cations. When glass basicity increases103, the incorporation (solubility) of high field
             strength cations increases.

              5.A.2.a.5.f. Incorporation of Zr4+ Cations in Silicate Glasses Structure
              The structural environment of Zr4+ ions in silicate and in aluminoborosilicate glasses
          was widely studied by Zr EXAFS and XANES spectroscopies61 [302, 450]. In these glass
            compositions, Zr was 6-coordinated to oxygen anions and bond valence  - bond length
             considerations coupled with EXAFS results indicated that ZrO6 octahedra share corners with
           SiO4 tetrahedra (existence of Zr-O-Si bonds with a mean Zr-O-Si angle of about 160-170°)119.
            Figure 100a shows that Zr4+ ions cannot bond directly to a BO connecting two SiO4
              tetrahedra. Indeed, in this situation and if the Si-O distance remains similar to that occurring
             in silica and alkali silicate glasses (RSiO = 1.62Å and SSiO = 1.01), the oxygen anion would be
             strongly overbonded (SZrO + 2SSiO = 2.68 v.u. > 2 v.u.). To make possible such a local
           environment around Zr, the bonding between Zr and a BO would require a significant
            lengthening of Si-O bonds beyond their observed maximum values in aluminosilicates (1.54-
           1.70Å [459]). Indeed, in these conditions (SZrO + 2SSiO = 2.00 v.u.), SSiO = 0.66 v.u. which
            implies that RSiO = 1.77Å > 1.70Å according to equation (11) with R0(Si) = 1.624Å. Such Si-
       O bonds lengthening would lead to disruption of the silicate network and thus Zr4+ cations
           can be only bonded to NBOs (Figure 100b,c).
                 Nevertheless, if we consider only two next nearest high field strength cations (one Zr4+
           and one Si4+) in the neighborhood of an oxygen anion engaged in a Zr-O-Si bond (Figure

                Numerous dynamic (i.e. with permanent or periodic solution renewal) and static (i.e. without solution renewal)

                    the beginning of glass alteration will be about only 50°C [51] or 30°C [404]. Even if the high-flow rate Soxhlet
                       tests in which glass samples are exposed to large volumes of distilled water (T = 100°C) are not representative
                    of the alteration conditions that would occur for nuclear glasses in repository environment because they are far
                 from solution saturation, such tests enables to determine the initial alteration rate r0 of the glass. By comparison,
                    the static leaching tests performed in relatively small volumes of solution (at T ≤ 90°C) are more representative
                    of repository environment because the leachant may become saturated with specific constituents from the glass.
                   Indeed, groundwater  is expected to slowly migrate from the environment to the nuclear glass and after
                   corrosion the contaminated water is expected to slowly migrate from the glass to the environment [536]. Static
                   leaching tests are used to follow the evolution with time of the glass dissolution kinetics. In order to reach more
                    rapidly saturation phenomena, static alteration tests are generally performed on powdered glass samples at very
                  high surface-to-volume (S/V) ratios. The fact that during leaching tests in laboratories, the temperature is
                    generally higher (90-100°C) than the true temperature during nuclear glasses alteration by groundwater (50°C),
                   enables to increase leaching kinetic. Indeed, leach rates increase by two orders of magnitude between 25 and
                100°C [9]. It is generally observed that glass alteration rate decreases with time in closed systems (static
                      alteration conditions) but becomes constant with time in flowing systems (Soxhlet tests for instance) if there are

             5.A.2.b. Structural Role and Effect on Nuclear Glass Properties of Al2O3 and B2O3

                In paragraph 5.A.2.a. we mainly focussed on the structural role and on the impact on
            nuclear glass properties of SiO2 which is the main network-forming oxide in borosilicate
            nuclear glasses and of several of the main network-modifying and intermediate oxides (alkali
             oxides, alkaline-earth oxides, molybdenum oxide, zirconium oxide, rare-earth oxides and
             actinide oxides) present either in HLW solutions or in the glass frit used to prepare nuclear
              glasses. In this paragraph, we will now focus on the structural role and on the effect on
            nuclear glass properties of two other oxides Al2O3 and B2O3. These two oxides that are
             present in almost all commercial [53, 333, 334, 442] and defence borosilicate nuclear glasses
              [9, 30, 51] have an important impact on the distribution of the low field strength network-
           modifying alkali and alkaline-earth cations and also - according to glass composition - on the
              distribution of high field strength cations such as rare-earth cations (and probably also on Pu
           and minor actinides distribution) in glass structure. These two oxides also have a significant
             influence on nuclear glasses chemical durability.

            This evolution of melt properties facilitates melting and fining at lower temperature which
            enables to prepare nuclear glasses at temperature as low as 1100-1150°C. Nevertheless, it is
            important to underline that for a given temperature, the increase of boric oxide concentration
             in the melt may induce an important increase of its volatility41 (as alkali oxides, boric oxide is
           one of the most volatile constituent in the composition of nuclear glasses [51]). The same
              effect on η at high temperature and on Tliquidus could also be obtained by increasing alkali
            oxide  content  as  seen  in  §5.A.2.a.2.  However,  this  would  induce  an  increasing
            depolymerization of the glass  silicate network that could be more deleterious to glass
            chemical durability than the introduction of B2O3141 (increase of the proportion of poorly
            durable NBO- and alkali cation-rich regions in glass structure) and a decrease of Tg that could
           be problematic  for nuclear  glasses during  interim  storage  if  the  glass  transformation
            temperature becomes lower than the temperature in the bulk of glass canisters due to the
            heating produced by radionuclides decay  (risks of  crystallization). In comparison, the
             introduction of B2O3 generally leads to an increase of Tg 141 which is well known for Pyrex®
              glass. Thus, boric oxide raises melt viscosity at low temperature (near Tg) and reduces it at
            high temperature (near and above  Tliquidus), as a result glass makers said that the "glass
           becomes shorter" with B2O3 addition142. For the reasons indicated above, this is beneficial to
            nuclear waste vitrification. Another interesting point is that boron rarely enters the crystalline
            phases that may form in the supercooled melt and remains in the residual glass phase [51].

            a poorly durable  alkali- and  alkaline-earth-rich  borate phase  in  the supercooled melt
             (metastable  liquid-liquid phase  separation). Borosilicate nuclear glass compositions are
             generally formulated in order to avoid such phase separation phenomena during melt cooling

             5.A.2.b.2.c. B2O3 in Borosilicate and Aluminoborosilicate Glasses
                In previous paragraphs, we considered separately the two network-forming oxides SiO2
           and B2O3 in silicate and borate glasses. In this paragraph, we will now consider glasses
            containing both boron and silicon in their compositions. The case of glasses containing at the
          same time SiO2, B2O3 and Al2O3 (these three oxides playing a network-forming role in the
             structure of nuclear glasses) will be only briefly presented in this paragraph but an example of
             glass containing these three oxides with other components is widely detailed in §5.C.
              Because of the numerous applications of alkali borosilicate glasses (laboratory glassware,
            pharmaceutical glassware, household cooking utensils, nuclear waste forms…) and because
            small amounts of B2O3 are frequently added to silicate glass compositions either to facilitate
            melting or to improve their properties (thermal insulation wool, E-glass fibers to reinforce
               plastic, liquid crystal display sheet...), a considerable literature exist on the structural role of
          B2O3 in borosilicate glasses using mainly NMR spectroscopy [615-621]. As it is not the aim
             of this paragraph to give a review of the current knowledge of how boron may enter silicate
           network and how  it can affect glass properties, we will only present several of the main
              results that can useful to understand the structure and the properties of borosilicate nuclear
              glasses.
                In borate glasses, we saw that boron can exist either as BO3 triangles (isolated or in
            boroxol entities) with or without NBOs or as BO4 tetrahedral units charge balanced by alkali
              cations. In silicate glasses, we saw that various Qn (SiO4) units can be simultaneously present
             in glass structure and that alkali cations are located near NBOs to charge balance their
            negative charge. Consequently, we can expect that the structure of glasses containing both
            SiO2, B2O3 and alkali oxides is very complex. We will first briefly consider the case of B2O3
           added to SiO2 (binary glass) before envisaging the case of the ternary SiO2-B2O3-Na2O
            system.

            Molybdenum is one of the most abundant fission product formed in nuclear reactors
            during the production of electricity (Tables 4 and 5) [1]. After reprocessing of nuclear spent

            conditioning in highly durable  borosilicate glassy  matrices157. Lutze indicated  that the
              solubility of Mo in borosilicate nuclear glasses was relatively low (~ 1 wt% MoO3) which

           5.B.2. Molybdenum in Glasses

                In this chapter (see §5.A.2.a.5.e) we already presented several data on the incorporation of
          molybdenum  (as Mo6+ cations)  in  silicate  glasses. Several information on Mo-bearing
            phosphate glasses and on molybdate glasses without traditional network-forming oxide19,157
           were also given. In this paragraph, we summarize and present complementary information on
             the incorporation of molybdate entities in the structure of silicate and borosilicate glasses and
          on the similitude between the local environment around Mo6+ cations in these glasses and in
           molybdate crystals.
                In silicate and borosilicate glasses, molybdenum may exist under different oxidation
               states: Mo6+, Mo5+, Mo4+ and Mo3+ cations. However, if these glasses are prepared under
             oxidizing or neutral atmosphere, molybdenum mainly occurred at oxidation state +VI which
                is the most stable oxidation state of molybdenum [650, 652, 659, 661]. Mo6+ is a high field
              strength165 network-modifier cation (Table 32) known to be only slightly soluble in silicate
           and borosilicate glasses and to induce glass-in-glass phase separation and crystallization in
            supercooled melts during cooling [114, 376]. Indeed, because of its high field strength, Mo6+
             cation exerts a strong ordering effect on the surrounding oxygen anions and may easily
             separate from the silicate or borosilicate glassy network combining with other elements such
             as alkali and alkaline-earth cations to form crystalline molybdates [38, 652, 657, 658].
           Concerning the structural role of molybdenum in silicate and borosilicate glasses, X-ray
            absorption  spectroscopy showed  that  hexavalent molybdenum  cations  are  located  in
             tetrahedral MoO4 2- entities within alkali and alkaline-earth rich depolymerized regions outside
             the silicate or borosilicate network (i.e., the oxygen atoms of MoO42- units are not directly
           bounded to Si or B, see also the bond valence-bond length considerations summarized in
            Figure 98) [146, 286, 453, 454]. In Figure 121, we propose a schematic representation of the
             structure of a soda-lime borosilicate glass showing the location of MoO42- entities in the
           depolymerized regions (i.e., in regions rich in both NBOs and (Na+,Ca2+) cations) of the
             glassy network. The same kind of isolated MoO42- molybdate tetrahedral entities are presentreserved.                                   166             in  the Na2MoO4   and CaMoO4  (powellite)167 phases  that can  crystallize  in  nuclear

             5.B.3.b. Stuctural Characterization of Mo-rich Borosilicate Glasses

             5.B.3.b.1. Oxidation State of Molybdenum in Glasses
               Before characterization of glass structure (i.e., study of Si, B, Na and Mo environments by
       NMR and Raman spectroscopies), the oxidation state of molybdenum cations in Mx and By
             glass series was studied by EPR at X band (9.51 GHz). Indeed, a fraction of molybdenum
         may be present at oxidation states lower than +VI.
            As Mo6+ cations are diamagnetic (electronic configuration 4d0), they cannot be detected
          by EPR. Nevertheless, the presence of Mo5+ (4d1) or Mo3+ (4d3) paramagnetic cations was
             detected by EPR in numerous papers concerning silicate and borosilicate [452, 650, 659,
             661], phosphate [666-673] and borate [667, 674, 675] glasses.
              For all glasses of Mx and By series, EPR spectra revealed the existence of a signal due to
          molybdenum centered near g=1.913 detected from 20K to room temperature (Figure 124a).
         No signal associated with Mo3+ (4d3) cations near g~5.19 was observed [452, 666]. The
              characteristics of the EPR signal indicated that it could be attributed to Mo5+ cations located
             in low symmetry sites as the spin-lattice relaxation time of d1 ions is known to increase with
               site distortion enabling to detect their EPR signals at high temperature [196]. The presence of
            a small intensity hyperfine structure on EPR spectra (Figure 124a), that can be attributed to
             the contribution of 95Mo and 97Mo isotopes with nuclear spin I=5/2, confirmed that the signal
              at g=1.913 was due to molybdenum and not to other paramagnetic impurities.

             5.B.3.c.3.a. By series
            As BO4 units are known to be preferentially charge compensated by alkali cations rather
            than by alkaline-earth cations, the distribution of these cations in the borosilicate network of
          By glasses (and melts) is affected when y increases. This structural evolution is probably at
             the origin of the effect of increasing B2O3 concentration on molybdenum crystallization and
          more particularly on the nature and on of the proportion of molybdate crystals (disappearance
             of sodium molybdate and increase of the amount of powellite). Indeed, these results can be
            explained if we consider that the relative proportion of calcium in the depolymerized regions
             of glass structure (Figure 121) increases by increasing boron oxide concentration because
            both the quantity of BO4 units increases and these units are preferentially charge compensated
          by Na+ cations rather than by Ca2+ cations. It is thus easy to understand that when y increases,
             the depolymerized domains  in which MoO42-  units  are  located  in  the  melt become
             progressively depleted in sodium and the local concentration ratio [CaO]/[Na2O] in these
           domains increases. Indeed, if we admit that the BO4 units detected by MAS NMR are charge
           compensated only by Na+ ions, the Na2O concentration available for the charge compensation
             of MoO42- units would decrease across the By series (in mol%): 16.40 (B0), 11.79 (B6), 7.71
              (B12), 4.21 (B18) and 1.00 (B24). (see the [Na+]/[BO4] concentration ratio evolution in Figure
            136, see also Figure 131 showing that the 23Na NMR parameters of B2O3-rich By (y=18 and
            24) glasses are very close to that of the B0.2Na reference glass). In these conditions and for all
          By samples, the quantity of CaO available for charge compensation strongly exceeds that of
          MoO3. Indeed, the [CaO]/[MoO3] concentration ratio (in mol%) only decreases from 4.81
             (B0) to 3.52 (B24) with the increase of B2O3 concentration. Consequently, when the amount of
           boron oxide increases, the average field strength of cations in the depolymerized regions
             increases (because of their charge +2, Ca2+ cation has a higher field strength than Na+ cation
            (Table 32)) and thus the tendency of the high field strength Mo6+ cations to separate from thereserved.
             glass structure and to form calcium molybdate crystals (i.e., powellite) increases.

           5.C.7. Conclusions of the Study of a New RE-rich Glass for the Immobization
           of Concentrated Highly Radioactive Wastes

                In conclusion to all the studies performed on the structure and crystallization tendency of
             the RE-rich glasses A, AS and  all the simplified glass  series derived from glass AS
            composition  belonging  to  the  SiO2-B2O3-Al2O3-Na2O-CaO-ZrO2-RE2O3  system  and
           developed to immobilize higher concentration of high level nuclear wastes than current
              borosilicate nuclear glasses, the main following points were shown:

             −   After a preliminary research [14] on several RE-rich aluminoborosilicate complex
                  and simplified series of glasses able to incorporated high waste concentrations, a
                  complex peralkaline glass A (and a simplified version of this glass referred to as
                      glass AS) composition was selected as good glassy matrix for the immobilization of
                    highly concentrated HLW solutions (Table 50). During these preliminary  tests,
                     several compositions were very prone to devitrification during natural cooling of the
                    melt or heat treatments of the glass in a RE-apatite phase able to incorporate minor
                      actinides (with composition close to Ca2RE8(SiO4)6O2) and it has been shown that
                   only the lowest Al2O3 content glasses were stable. Indeed, it is very important that
                     nuclear glass A composition was optimized to avoid the formation of RE-rich big
                       crystals during the melt cooling or during the storage of nuclear glass canisters.
                    Indeed, such big crystals could then swell under the α-decay of minor actinides
                  which could then generate glass fracturation that would lead to an increase of the
                      specific area of the waste form.
             −  With  increasing RE2O3  concentration (RE=Nd  or  La), EXAFS showed  that
                neodymium cations were surrounded by 8 ± 1 oxygen atoms and ~ 3.5 second

                 Nd2O3 concentration increased. Only a slight increase in Nd-sites distribution was
